name: AI capability
question: Which kinds of useful work can AI complete, with what reliability, human support, and evaluation uncertainty?
synthesis: This bounded scoping scan finds substantial progress on several prepared digital-task benchmarks, alongside persistent difficulty with open-ended work, reliable execution, and knowing when outputs are wrong. Scores depend on task selection, tools, context, grading and model vintage; workplace experiments can therefore show benefits or slowdowns without contradicting benchmark gains. METR's public time-horizon series is no longer actively updated, and neither its human-time units nor composite capability scores establish how much of a job can be delegated safely.

facets.label: Breadth and capability trends
facets.description: Changes across model generations and domains, including what composite scores can and cannot establish.

facets.label: Task completion and reliability
facets.description: End-to-end success, consistency, robustness, calibration, failure severity and human-equivalent task difficulty.

facets.label: Workflows and usable deliverables
facets.description: Repository changes, computer use, professional artifacts, coordination and organizational context.

facets.label: Scientific and mathematical work
facets.description: Expert questions, data analysis, research judgment and the distinction between benchmark answers and discoveries.

facets.label: Human assistance and productivity
facets.description: Whether using AI improves actual completion time and quality, including review costs and dependence on task fit.

facets.label: Measurement validity
facets.description: Contamination, flawed answer keys, construct validity, grading, scaffolds, denominator changes and uncertainty.

sources.title: Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models
sources.authors: METR; foundational study by Thomas Kwa et al.
sources.design: Repeated model evaluations; logistic task-success curves fitted against expert human completion times.
sources.population: Selected software engineering, machine-learning and cybersecurity tasks; expert baseliners and frontier model-agent configurations.
sources.geography: Digital tasks; no representative country population.
sources.duration: Models released from 2019 onward; TH1.0 and TH1.1; public page last updated September 8, 2026.
sources.measure: Human task duration at fitted 50% or 80% success, with bootstrap uncertainty; not agent runtime.
sources.finding: The page explicitly says it is no longer actively updated. Historical evaluations show increasing task horizons, but the current page warns estimates above 16 human-hours are unreliable for its task suite.
sources.limitations: Prepared, well-specified technical tasks; sparse long tasks; model coverage selective; human timings use successful attempts and often low prior context. No direct job-automation estimate.
sources.locator: Last updated; Methodological Details; Frequently Asked Questions; warning above task plot
sources.sourceNote: Read official status, methods and FAQ. Also checked arXiv:2503.14499v4 (July 10, 2026) metadata and selected paper text. No live chart values inferred from unloaded controls; original study and release updates are consolidated here.
sources.selectionReason: An interpretable repeated measure with explicit scope, uncertainty and maintenance status.
sources.headline: Longer technical tasks, with limits on precision and current coverage
sources.searchOrigin: Seed collections; query: site.metr.org time horizons paused updates 2026; official page and linked paper.

sources.title: Research note: Clarifying limitations of time horizon
sources.authors: Thomas Kwa
sources.design: Benchmark author's methodological interpretation and limitations note, not a new evaluation series.
sources.population: METR task-horizon estimates and their interpretation.
sources.geography: Not applicable.
sources.duration: January 22, 2026 note reflecting on the preceding nine months.
sources.measure: Meaning of reliability thresholds, task duration, human baselines and domain transfer.
sources.finding: The author rejects interpreting a horizon as unattended runtime or a general delegation threshold. Baseline conventions, task selection and domain differences materially affect its meaning.
sources.limitations: Author interpretation; explicitly less reviewed than METR research posts. Some supporting comparisons are cited rather than newly estimated here.
sources.locator: Bullets: Time horizon is not precise; Time horizon differs between domains; Benchmark vs real-world task distribution
sources.sourceNote: Inspected the methodological arguments, cautions and numerical examples; did not independently reproduce cited domain evaluations.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed collections; direct official note.

sources.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
sources.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein
sources.design: Randomized issue-level trial allowing or disallowing AI on developers' own repositories.
sources.population: 16 experienced open-source developers completing 246 real issues.
sources.geography: Open-source repositories; participant-country distribution not established in inspected summary.
sources.duration: February-June 2025; tasks averaged approximately two hours; published July 10, 2025.
sources.measure: Implementation time with AI access versus without, using recordings and reported time.
sources.finding: AI-allowed tasks took 19% longer in this sample; the reported confidence interval was +2% to +39%. This is a negative productivity finding for early-2025 tools in a specific experienced-developer setting.
sources.limitations: Small, selected developer sample and familiar, mature repositories; tools and workflow are dated. Not evidence that all coding assistance reduces productivity.
sources.locator: Methodology; opening result; February 2026 update for confidence interval
sources.sourceNote: Read official experiment summary and subsequent update. Full underlying trial paper and raw recordings were not reviewed.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed collections; official study summary and linked uplift update.

sources.title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
sources.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud
sources.design: Follow-up randomized-task experiment with returning and newly recruited developers, accompanied by a redesign proposal.
sources.population: Original participants who returned plus newly recruited open-source developers; not an unchanged panel.
sources.geography: Open-source development; country coverage not established.
sources.duration: New experiment began August 2025; update published February 24, 2026.
sources.measure: Relative completion time; participation and time-measurement problems.
sources.finding: Raw estimates favor faster work, but intervals include no effect. Authors consider them unreliable because developers increasingly decline AI-free work, pay changed, and concurrent agents complicate time accounting.
sources.limitations: Selection into participation and task inclusion prevents a clean trend comparison with the early-2025 trial. Authors' belief in greater acceleration is not a precise causal estimate.
sources.locator: Opening explanation; raw results; discussion of selection effects
sources.sourceNote: Inspected official follow-up and design-change explanation. Classified as repeated mixed-cohort evidence, not a uniform longitudinal panel or a validated replacement series.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed collections; original trial's update link.

sources.title: Summary of METR's predeployment evaluation of Claude Opus 5.5
sources.authors: METR
sources.design: Predeployment task testing supplemented with a developer questionnaire, interview and a separate internal assessment.
sources.population: One model on five AI research and development tasks, plus contextual evidence about Anthropic.
sources.geography: AI laboratory research context; no population sampling.
sources.duration: API testing over 10 business days; published September 22, 2026.
sources.measure: Performance on verifiable and judgment-intensive research tasks; qualitative assessment of research acceleration.
sources.finding: METR reports incremental improvement over Fable 5.1 and continuing research-judgment weaknesses; it considers full AI R&D automation unlikely on this evidence.
sources.limitations: Preliminary, narrow testing. Supporting evidence from a separate privileged-access team was unavailable even to this report's team; Anthropic reviewed and edited the summary before METR approval.
sources.locator: Note on independence; Summary of evidence; Conclusions (A)
sources.sourceNote: Read public evaluation summary, not confidential internal evidence or the full system card. Retained as a bounded recent update, not a time-horizon datapoint.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed collections; direct METR publication.

sources.title: Epoch Capabilities Index: series and methodology
sources.authors: Epoch AI; frontier-trend analysis by Alexander Barry
sources.design: Composite index fitted to overlapping model-benchmark scores using an item-response-style logistic model with regularization.
sources.population: Models and benchmarks included by Epoch; combines creator, developer and Epoch evaluations.
sources.geography: International model developers; benchmark coverage is not geographically representative work.
sources.duration: Retrospective model-release comparisons; inspected September 1, 2026 trend analysis and documentation available October 22, 2026.
sources.measure: Latent capability on an arbitrary anchored scale, with bootstrap intervals; domain-specific variants available.
sources.finding: Epoch reports faster frontier-score growth after reasoning models appeared. Index points are not percentages of tasks or output, and the fit itself does not assume a time trend.
sources.limitations: Changing benchmark mix, uneven score availability, common-factor assumptions and heterogeneous evaluation settings affect comparisons. Specialized abilities may be obscured.
sources.locator: ECI documentation: Overview and Methodology; eci-frontier-trend opening paragraphs
sources.sourceNote: Read https://epoch.ai/data/eci-documentation/methodology and https://epoch.ai/data-insights/eci-frontier-trend. Live leaderboard remained Loading in text extraction; no newest-model ranking inferred.
sources.selectionReason: Tracks broad progress across saturated and unsaturated benchmarks, provided the arbitrary scale and source mix are visible.
sources.headline: A broad capability trend, not a percentage of work automated
sources.searchOrigin: Seed ECI entry; official dashboard, documentation and frontier-trend article.

sources.title: Remote Labor Index: Measuring AI Automation of Remote Work, with creator updates
sources.authors: Mantas Mazeika et al.; Center for AI Safety and Scale AI
sources.design: Repeated agent evaluations on freelance projects, with expert comparison against accepted professional deliverables.
sources.population: 240 curated projects across 23 Upwork domains; documentation describes 230 private quantitative-evaluation projects and 10 public examples.
sources.geography: Online freelance market; not a probability sample of global workers or occupations.
sources.duration: Initial paper October 30, 2025; inspected July 1, 2026 creator update and current leaderboard documentation.
sources.measure: Share of deliverables judged client-acceptable relative to the professional reference; pairwise quality and cost measures.
sources.finding: Initial performance was low; creator updates show improvement with newer models and stronger scaffolds. The July update also finds an automated grader overstates absolute success on newer models.
sources.limitations: Excludes client interaction, teamwork and long-term evaluation. Model and scaffold effects change together. Denominator consistency between reported rates and documented private set needs reconciliation.
sources.locator: Paper sections 3.2-3.4 and 5; leaderboard Dataset Design; creator update section 3
sources.sourceNote: Inspected arXiv:2510.26787v1 and https://safe.ai/blog/significant-increase-in-digital-labor-automation. Omitted exact success-rate comparisons because the inspected update does not clearly restate its scored denominator; launch narrative is not a current frontier score.
sources.selectionReason: Adds multimodal paid-project evidence beyond coding, with explicit acceptance criteria and important generalization limits.
sources.headline: Freelance deliverables improve, but client-ready completion remains demanding
sources.searchOrigin: Seed RLI leaderboard and CAIS update; followed original paper.

sources.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
sources.authors: Tejal Patwardhan et al.
sources.design: One-off benchmark introduction comparing professional and model deliverables with expert grading and controlled context/scaffold variations.
sources.population: 44 occupations in nine large US sectors; 30 tasks per occupation, with a 220-task public gold subset.
sources.geography: US occupational and industry selection; digital knowledge work.
sources.duration: Launch September 25, 2025; paper v1 October 5, 2025; no workplace follow-up.
sources.measure: Expert preference for model versus professional deliverables; modeled cost/time scenarios; context and reasoning-effort sensitivity.
sources.finding: The evaluated frontier models approach professional deliverable quality on some tasks. Context, reasoning effort and scaffolding affect scores; estimated savings depend on assumed human review and retry workflows.
sources.limitations: Precisely specified one-shot tasks exclude much tacit context, interaction and physical work. Automated grading has self-preference and modality limitations; projected savings are not a field productivity experiment.
sources.locator: Sections 3.1-3.3, 5 and A.6.2-A.6.3
sources.sourceNote: Inspected methods, results and limitations plus launch page. Text adjacent to the 47.6% result inconsistently says just over half; omitted numerical headline pending figure-level reconciliation.
sources.selectionReason: Broad occupational deliverables complement technical benchmarks, with design and grading caveats directly documented.
sources.headline: Prepared professional deliverables are becoming feasible; whole jobs are untested
sources.searchOrigin: Seed GDPval article and arXiv paper; consolidated duplicate launch and paper records.

sources.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
sources.authors: Carlos E. Jimenez, John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, Karthik Narasimhan
sources.design: Benchmark construction and baseline evaluation using real issue-pull-request pairs and executable tests.
sources.population: 2,294 issues from 12 Python repositories.
sources.geography: Public GitHub projects; not a sample of all software employment.
sources.duration: Original October 2023 evaluation; inspected v3 dated November 11, 2024.
sources.measure: Fraction of repository issues resolved under the specified test harness.
sources.finding: The original best baseline solved 1.96% of the 2,294 issues. This established a difficult repository-level task; it is not a current frontier score.
sources.limitations: Python-only original sample; passing tests does not ensure maintainable, efficient or complete code. Public issues and patches create later contamination risk.
sources.locator: Abstract; section 7 Discussion
sources.sourceNote: Inspected baseline description and discussion. Original SWE-bench, Verified, Pro and later leaderboards are not treated as interchangeable denominators.
sources.searchOrigin: Foundational coding-benchmark extension to seed SWE-bench Pro and Verified audit.

sources.title: SWE-Bench Pro: benchmark design and leaderboard
sources.authors: Scale AI research team
sources.design: Repeated repository-task evaluations using engineered environments, issue/commit harvesting and regression tests.
sources.population: Public, held-out open-source and private proprietary codebase subsets; inspected public-set documentation.
sources.geography: Software repositories; geography of contributors not established.
sources.duration: Benchmark introduced in 2025; current documentation inspected October 22, 2026.
sources.measure: Task resolution under specified agent and test setup, reported by benchmark subset.
sources.finding: The design broadens codebase and task coverage and uses private or copyleft repositories to reduce contamination risk. Launch comparisons indicate greater difficulty than Verified.
sources.limitations: Licensing is not proof of absence from training. Public and private subsets, agent scaffolds and versions must be kept distinct; launch narrative is stale for current rankings.
sources.locator: Overview; Methodology; source URL redirects from swe_bench_pro_public
sources.sourceNote: Read official design page; linked paper landing page lacked extractable body. No dynamic leaderboard result or sample denominator asserted.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed public leaderboard; followed redirect and official paper link.

sources.title: Why SWE-bench Verified no longer measures frontier coding capabilities
sources.authors: OpenAI
sources.design: Targeted audit of frequently failed Verified problems plus probes for reproduction of reference solutions and problem details.
sources.population: A failure-enriched subset covering 27.6% of SWE-bench Verified; tested frontier models.
sources.geography: Public code benchmark; not population-based.
sources.duration: Audit published February 23, 2026.
sources.measure: Defective tests and evidence of benchmark exposure in models.
sources.finding: At least 59.4% of audited problems had tests rejecting functionally correct submissions. The denominator is the selected failure-prone subset, not the entire benchmark; the audit also found reproduction evidence consistent with contamination.
sources.limitations: Selection prevents treating the defect proportion as a full-dataset estimate. Provider-led audit and incomplete training-data visibility limit attribution.
sources.locator: Background; Too narrow and too wide tests; Contamination
sources.sourceNote: Inspected official audit explanation and its sampling qualifier. Stopping this benchmark does not imply that all observed coding progress was spurious.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed official Verified audit.

sources.title: GAIA: a benchmark for General AI Assistants
sources.authors: Gregoire Mialon, Clementine Fourrier, Craig Swift, Thomas Wolf, Yann LeCun, Thomas Scialom
sources.design: Human-created questions requiring browsing, tools and multimodal reasoning, with human validation and model baselines.
sources.population: 466 questions across three difficulty levels; independent validation annotators.
sources.geography: Digital assistant tasks; no representative country sample.
sources.duration: November 2023 benchmark release; individual short task attempts, no follow-up.
sources.measure: Correct final answer; human annotator validation performance and task duration.
sources.finding: Original human validation accuracy was much higher than tool-equipped model accuracy. Even conceptually simple questions exposed failures in multi-step execution.
sources.limitations: Final-answer grading omits process safety; human baseline is validation annotators on retained valid questions. Plugins were manually selected for a model baseline and cannot be reproduced exactly.
sources.locator: Section 6; appendix validation protocol and Tables 3-4
sources.sourceNote: Read original methodology, baseline qualifications and limitations. Repeated stochastic runs in one experiment do not make this a longitudinal population study.
sources.searchOrigin: Requested GAIA coverage; primary paper and full HTML.

sources.title: OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments
sources.authors: Tianbao Xie et al.
sources.design: Execution-evaluated computer-use tasks in real desktop applications with reproducible initial states.
sources.population: 369 main Ubuntu tasks, including single-app and multi-app workflows; supplementary Windows tasks.
sources.geography: Desktop applications; no workforce sampling.
sources.duration: April 2024 release; inspected May 30, 2024 v2; short task attempts.
sources.measure: Successful completion assessed by task-specific scripts.
sources.finding: The original best model achieved 12.24% success on the main benchmark, versus reported human performance of 72.36%; GUI grounding and operational knowledge were major problems.
sources.limitations: Historical baselines, not current computer-use capability. App versions and step budgets matter; scripts can have false positives and negatives despite repeated quality checks.
sources.locator: Abstract; section 3.3 and Table 3; evaluation-quality discussion
sources.sourceNote: Read original paper's benchmark composition and quality-control text. Replaced seed's secondary AI Index pointer with original source.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed OSWorld secondary pointer; retrieved arXiv:2404.07972.

sources.title: GPQA: A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark
sources.authors: David Rein, Betty Li Hou, Asa Cooper Stickland, Jackson Petty, Richard Yuanzhe Pang, Julien Dirani, Julian Michael, Samuel R. Bowman
sources.design: Expert-authored and validated multiple-choice science benchmark with expert, nonexpert and model baselines.
sources.population: 448 biology, chemistry and physics questions; graduate-level expert validators.
sources.geography: English-language academic questions; no representative scientist population.
sources.duration: November 20, 2023 v1; one-off baseline assessment.
sources.measure: Answer accuracy; retrospective treatment of identified human mistakes.
sources.finding: The original GPT-4 baseline reached 39% accuracy on the benchmark. Expert performance depended on whether retrospectively identified mistakes were excluded.
sources.limitations: Closed-ended knowledge assessment does not establish research execution, novelty or practical laboratory skill. Historical baseline and non-identical human/model conditions.
sources.locator: Abstract; submission history
sources.sourceNote: Primary abstract and metadata only. Full methods were not inspected; no current GPQA Diamond score imported.
sources.searchOrigin: Query: GPQA FrontierMath benchmark arxiv; original GPQA record.

sources.title: FrontierMath: A Benchmark for Evaluating Advanced Mathematical Reasoning in AI
sources.authors: Elliot Glazer et al.
sources.design: Original unpublished mathematics problems constructed and vetted by specialists, with automatically verifiable answers.
sources.population: Hundreds of advanced problems across mathematical fields.
sources.geography: International mathematical expertise; not a sampled national population.
sources.duration: Original November 7, 2024 release; latest inspected metadata v7, December 23, 2025.
sources.measure: Problem-solving success under the benchmark protocol.
sources.finding: Introduces difficult expert-created problems intended to retain discrimination beyond earlier mathematics tests and reduce public-data contamination.
sources.limitations: Answer verification is not the same as proof quality or original research. Abstract's historical low-score statement should not be presented as current; later tiers and open-problem variants differ.
sources.locator: Abstract; submission history
sources.sourceNote: Abstract and version history inspected, not full paper or current dynamic leaderboard. No current success-rate claim retained.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed Epoch benchmark hub; query: GPQA FrontierMath benchmark arxiv.

sources.title: LAB-Bench: Measuring Capabilities of Language Models for Biology Research
sources.authors: Jon M. Laurent, Joseph D. Janizek, Michael Ruzo, Michaela M. Hinks, Michael J. Hammerling, Siddharth Narayanan, Manvitha Ponnapati, Andrew D. White, Samuel G. Rodriques
sources.design: Biology-research task benchmark with multiple-choice questions, abstention measures and expert comparison.
sources.population: More than 2,400 questions involving literature, figures, databases, sequences and protocols; PhD-level biologists.
sources.geography: Scientific tasks; no country-representative researcher sample.
sources.duration: July 2024 evaluation; inspected v3 dated July 17, 2024.
sources.measure: Accuracy, precision and coverage across subdomains, including an option not to answer.
sources.finding: Human experts substantially outperformed tested models overall. Variation across subdomains makes a single science score insufficient.
sources.limitations: Human experts could use tools; tested models lacked comparable tools. Prompt sensitivity, distractor quality and small human-evaluation subsets constrain comparisons; not laboratory execution.
sources.locator: Sections 2.2-2.4 and 3 Discussion and Limitations
sources.sourceNote: Inspected human/model comparison and limitation sections of original benchmark. No inference about later LAB-Bench versions.
sources.searchOrigin: Query: LAB-Bench Measuring Capabilities Language Models Biology Research 2024.

sources.title: ScienceAgentBench: Toward Rigorous Assessment of Language Agents for Data-Driven Scientific Discovery
sources.authors: Ziru Chen et al.
sources.design: Scientific code-generation tasks drawn from published studies; compares direct prompting, self-debug and an agent scaffold.
sources.population: 102 tasks from 44 papers in four disciplines, validated with nine subject specialists.
sources.geography: Bioinformatics, computational chemistry, geographic information science and psychology/neuroscience; no geographical population sample.
sources.duration: Original October 2024 study; inspected March 31, 2025 v3.
sources.measure: Task success, code similarity, execution validity and cost; with/without expert-provided knowledge.
sources.finding: Self-debugging improves performance for several models and can outperform a more elaborate scaffold. Expert context is not uniformly beneficial across metrics.
sources.limitations: Published-work reconstruction rather than novel discovery. Different reasoning budgets limit model comparisons. Abstract's best-agent claim omits higher o1-preview results shown in Table 3.
sources.locator: Sections 2-4; Table 3; human evaluation; appendix A
sources.sourceNote: Inspected task construction and table-level results. Avoided repeating abstract's 32.4% as the maximum across all displayed models because Table 3 reports higher o1-preview results with a budget caveat.
sources.searchOrigin: Query: ScienceAgentBench paper 2024; primary arXiv paper.

sources.title: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks
sources.authors: Frank F. Xu et al.
sources.design: Simulated workplace with tools, documents and model-simulated colleagues; agents evaluated against execution checkpoints.
sources.population: 175 tasks in a software-company environment.
sources.geography: Simulated digital organization; not observed production firms.
sources.duration: Initial December 2024 release; inspected September 10, 2025 v3.
sources.measure: Full-task success and partial-credit completion, with steps and inference cost.
sources.finding: In v3, Gemini 2.5 Pro completed 30.3% of the 175 tasks and obtained 39.3% partial-credit score. Full completion and partial progress are distinct outcomes.
sources.limitations: Simulated colleagues and one organization type; model comparisons use differing OpenHands versions. Does not measure sustained employment, customer outcomes or all organizational constraints.
sources.locator: Figure 1; sections 3-7; Table 1
sources.sourceNote: Read benchmark setup and revised result table. Treated as a revised one-off study, not an observed longitudinal workplace series.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed TheAgentCompany; retrieved latest listed v3.

sources.title: Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability
sources.authors: Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Peter Kirgis, Kangheng Liu, Saiteja Utpala, Arvind Narayanan
sources.design: Reliability framework operationalized in controlled, repeated-run and perturbation tests of model-agent configurations.
sources.population: 15 models across GAIA and tau-bench; one selected scaffold per benchmark.
sources.geography: Digital assistant and simulated service tasks; not representative deployment geography.
sources.duration: Retrospective comparison spanning 24 months of model releases; paper v3 June 2, 2026.
sources.measure: Twelve metrics covering consistency, robustness, predictability and safety; safety reported separately from aggregate reliability.
sources.finding: Large accuracy gains coincide with comparatively small reliability gains in this setup. Better average calibration need not improve identification of individual likely failures, particularly on GAIA.
sources.limitations: Only two benchmarks, one scaffold each and zero temperature; subjective metric normalization and model-based safety grading. Not evidence of an entire-field reliability plateau.
sources.locator: Sections 3-4 and 6; appendix G predictability analysis
sources.sourceNote: Inspected v3 methods, results and limitations. Earlier version had an outcome-consistency calculation correction, acknowledged by authors; dashboard and paper are not counted separately.
sources.selectionReason: Makes operational reliability measurable beyond average success; controlled comparison complements recurring capability series.
sources.headline: Higher accuracy does not ensure predictable, robust execution
sources.searchOrigin: Seed reliability tracker and arXiv:2602.16666; inspected latest v3.

sources.title: Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks
sources.authors: Andrew M. Bean et al.
sources.design: Systematic review by the source authors, with expert coding of benchmark papers and a construct-validity codebook.
sources.population: 445 benchmark papers selected from leading NLP and machine-learning conferences.
sources.geography: Research publication corpus, not representative world capability measurements.
sources.duration: Literature searched across conference years before November 2025; exact terminal year not extracted here.
sources.measure: Alignment among claimed phenomenon, tasks, scoring and interpretation; reviewer agreement.
sources.finding: The reviewed papers commonly exhibit weak operational definitions, representativeness problems or insufficient statistical support for comparisons; the authors propose eight recommendations.
sources.limitations: Conference and keyword coverage excludes other evaluation traditions; model-assisted screening and moderate coding agreement introduce review uncertainty. This dashboard scan is not itself systematic.
sources.locator: Sections 1 Methods, 2 Results and 4 Discussion; inclusion/exclusion appendix
sources.sourceNote: Read source review methods and synthesis, including its screening and double-coding qualifications. No claim that all AI benchmarks are invalid.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed Oxford summary; query: Measuring What Matters Construct Validity Large Language Model Benchmarks 2025; original paper.

sources.title: A benchmark of expert-level academic questions to assess AI capabilities
sources.authors: Center for AI Safety, Scale AI, HLE Contributors Consortium
sources.design: Expert-contributed multimodal, closed-ended questions filtered for difficulty, with model accuracy and calibration evaluation.
sources.population: 2,500 academic questions across dozens of subjects in the published description.
sources.geography: Global contributor network; English-centered benchmark is not a representative country-level test.
sources.duration: Benchmark originated in 2025; Nature publication January 28, 2026; static reported evaluations.
sources.measure: Answer correctness and confidence calibration, with tool and inference conditions distinguished.
sources.finding: Reported models have low accuracy and poor calibration on these expert questions. Correctness on closed-ended academic questions is a narrower construct than conducting original research.
sources.limitations: Adversarial difficulty selection and disputed answer keys complicate interpretation; evolving question revisions and tool access affect comparability.
sources.locator: Abstract; evaluation and calibration sections; Limitations
sources.sourceNote: Inspected publisher article's benchmark description and calibration discussion; no current leaderboard number asserted. Paired with independent Bio/Chem audit.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed HLE references; publisher result from foundational science benchmark search.

sources.title: About 30% of Humanity's Last Exam Chemistry/biology Answers are Likely Wrong
sources.authors: Michael Skarlinski, Jon Laurent, Albert Bou, Andrew White
sources.design: Expert and research-tool audit of answer-rationale pairs against scientific literature; later reports benchmark creators' follow-up.
sources.population: Text-only biology and chemistry subset of HLE, not all HLE questions.
sources.geography: Scientific question corpus; not population-based.
sources.duration: July 23, 2025 report, updated September 16, 2025.
sources.measure: Conflicting literature evidence and expert judgments of answer validity.
sources.finding: Audit identifies substantial answer-key problems; reported creator re-review uses a different adjudication procedure and finds a smaller problematic share. The disagreement itself requires version- and rubric-specific interpretation.
sources.limitations: No independent replication here; exact scored-item count and sampling details not recovered from inspected prose. Tool-assisted audit could have its own errors; cannot generalize the title to all HLE.
sources.locator: Opening audit result; September 16 update; worked examples and released-data discussion
sources.sourceNote: Read authors' report, not the complete item-level audit dataset. Numeric headline deliberately not restated as a field-wide or whole-benchmark error estimate.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed FutureHouse audit; corrected inaccessible non-www URL to official www version.

sources.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
sources.authors: Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Edward McFowland III, Ethan Mollick, Hila Lifshitz, Katherine C. Kellogg, Saran Rajendran, Lisa Krayer, Francois Candelon, Karim R. Lakhani
sources.design: Preregistered randomized experiment assigning consultants to no AI, GPT-4, or GPT-4 with an overview, on two task sets.
sources.population: 758 BCG consultants, predominantly early-career knowledge workers.
sources.geography: Global consulting firm; not representative national workforces.
sources.duration: Original experiment reported September 2023; inspected 2026 published revision; short experimental tasks, no sustained follow-up.
sources.measure: Human-graded quality, completion, time and correctness inside versus outside tested model competence.
sources.finding: AI improves quality and completion on suitable tasks, but reduces correctness on the deliberately challenging task while producing more persuasive/coherent answers.
sources.limitations: One firm, selected tasks and an early GPT-4 vintage; encouraged experimental use differs from voluntary adoption. Generalization depends on incentives and task mix.
sources.locator: Published PDF pp. 4-7; Tables 2, 4 and 10; discussion pp. 16-17
sources.sourceNote: 2023 seed landing/PDF returned 403; located and read author-hosted 2026 publication. Treated as one study across versions, without mixing older headline effect sizes into revised tables.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed HBS WP 24-013; query: Navigating the Jagged filetype:pdf site:hbs.edu.

sources.title: Can AI automate Epoch?
sources.authors: Kelly Hong, Greg Burnham
sources.design: Organization-specific work-task benchmark, one run per model-task combination with manual employee-standard grading.
sources.population: 11 Epoch work tasks across five categories; six model-agent systems.
sources.geography: One research organization; digital work.
sources.duration: Launch report October 8, 2026; one-shot evaluation, no follow-up.
sources.measure: Rubric quality and qualitative error analysis, including design, research planning and tacit conventions.
sources.finding: Leading models perform well on some well-defined tasks but struggle with experimental judgment, implicit standards and open-ended follow-through. Scores do not demonstrate organization-wide automation.
sources.limitations: Very small convenience task set and one run per task; evaluator-specific organizational standards; highest-setting harnesses differ across models.
sources.locator: Methodology: Tasks and Setup; Key findings; Limitations
sources.sourceNote: Read report methods, qualitative findings and small-sample warning. A benchmark launch is not yet a longitudinal organizational study.
sources.searchOrigin: Seed Can AI automate Epoch?; official October 2026 report.

sources.title: On the estimation and validity of AI time horizons: a statistical look at the METR plot
sources.authors: Drew T. Nguyen, William Fithian
sources.design: Statistical reanalysis of existing METR evaluations using monotone splines and item-response models with cross-validated scoring rules.
sources.population: 228 technical tasks and 26 AI systems from the reused dataset.
sources.geography: Technical benchmark data; no additional population sampling.
sources.duration: v1 submitted October 8, 2026; retrospective reanalysis, no new workplace follow-up.
sources.measure: Mapping between human completion time and model difficulty; predictive fit and construct-validity diagnostics.
sources.finding: The human-time/difficulty relationship is nonlinear in part of the observed range, so equal horizon multipliers need not mean equal capability gains. Authors also find the original aggregate fit can remain a useful ability measure.
sources.limitations: Fresh preprint and reused task distribution; superior predictive fit does not independently establish real-work external validity. Hypothetical longer-task curves are not observations.
sources.locator: Abstract; sections 2-3; section 4 Discussion
sources.sourceNote: Inspected model rationale and discussion, including qualified support for aggregate ability estimates. Not a new capability measurement series or blanket refutation of METR.
sources.searchOrigin: Query: site.metr.org time horizons paused updates 2026 surfaced statistical critique; retrieved original arXiv paper.

gaps.title: From prepared tasks to sustained work
gaps.summary: The reviewed benchmarks do not determine how much work can be delegated across extended, changing organizational workflows.
gaps.basis: GDPval and RLI improve realism but exclude major forms of interaction; TheAgentCompany simulates them, while Epoch's real-task sample is very small. Positive deliverable results coexist with a developer slowdown trial and a later selection-compromised update.
gaps.next: Follow the same teams and task queues over several model vintages, randomizing access where feasible and measuring accepted output, rework, review time and unresolved tasks over months.

gaps.title: Reliability at the point of delegation
gaps.summary: Average success and confidence are insufficient to establish which individual tasks users can safely delegate.
gaps.basis: METR's threshold is task-distribution-specific; GAIA grades final answers; the reliability study finds calibration and per-task failure discrimination can diverge. Its narrow benchmark/scaffold coverage limits broader inference.
gaps.next: Evaluate abstention and escalation policies on held-out workflows using repeated runs, environment shifts, failure severity, detection delay and total human recovery cost.

gaps.title: Stable progress measures despite changing tests
gaps.summary: Long-run comparisons need stronger links between benchmark versions, grading rules and model/scaffold configurations.
gaps.basis: ECI combines changing tests; METR's public series has stopped active updating; Verified and HLE audits identify test or answer problems. RLI updates change scaffolds, and the statistical horizon critique questions uniform interpretation of time multipliers without denying all progress.
gaps.next: Publish versioned bridge samples with frozen and refreshed tasks, independent adjudication, explicit scored denominators, contamination probes and model-by-scaffold crossover comparisons.

gaps.title: Scientific answers versus scientific contributions
gaps.summary: The reviewed science evidence measures several distinct steps but leaves their relationship to useful discoveries uncertain.
gaps.basis: GPQA, HLE and FrontierMath emphasize closed-ended answers; LAB-Bench tests research-related skills; ScienceAgentBench reconstructs published computational tasks. Epoch and METR's recent research evaluations expose judgment weaknesses despite strong performance on some verifiable work.
gaps.next: Prospectively evaluate blinded research projects with matched expert baselines, independent replication, novelty and decision-usefulness criteria, recording human intervention and failed research paths.

reviewNotes: Bounded, AI-assisted scoping scan, not a systematic review or human-reviewed bibliography. Source status records inspection depth, not correctness certification or study quality.
Publication year, version date, measurement period and checkedOn are different. Original benchmark results are historical even when an abstract page was revised later.
Selected sources comprise three repeated benchmark/index series and two one-off empirical evaluations. None is presented as a longitudinal worker or organizational panel.
METR's public chart is no longer actively updated as of its September 8, 2026 notice. This does not establish that all METR evaluation work has paused; September predeployment work continues.

RLI documentation says 240 total projects and 230 private quantitative projects. Public rates and later update denominators need reconciliation before extracting exact solved-project counts or plotting a continuous model-only trend.

GDPval section 3.1 juxtaposes 47.6% with a just-over-half sentence. ScienceAgentBench v3's abstract headline omits the higher o1-preview rows in Table 3. Numerical maxima were withheld rather than silently harmonized.

SWE-bench audit error proportions apply to a selected failure-enriched sample; HLE audit claims concern text-only biology/chemistry and evolving answer keys, not all HLE or all scientific evaluations.

Geographical diversity of capability evidence remains weaker than task/design diversity. English digital work, software and well-resourced research organizations dominate this selected corpus; this is a sample limitation, not proof of a whole-field absence.

Fulltext status means selected relevant methods/results/limitations were inspected, not that every appendix, dataset or code artifact was reproduced. GPQA and FrontierMath remain explicitly abstract-only.
